question: In a patient with confirmed elapid (cobra or krait) envenomation who is developing progressive ptosis and dysphagia, a neostigmine challenge with atropine pre-treatment is an appropriate adjunct to antivenom therapy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is TRUE. Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing ACh at the neuromuscular junction and partially overcoming post-synaptic (cobra-type) blockade. For pre-synaptic (krait-type) blockade the effect is less predictable, but a trial is warranted. Atropine 0.6 mg IV MUST precede neostigmine to block muscarinic overactivity. This intervention is always an ADJUNCT to ASV, not a replacement.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — TRUE. Neostigmine (an anticholinesterase) can partially reverse post-synaptic neurotoxic blockade — it is useful for cobra envenomation and worth trialling in krait envenomation. Atropine must be given FIRST to block the muscarinic side effects of neostigmine (bradycardia, hypersalivation, bronchospasm). This is a neostigmine-atropine challenge and is always adjunct to — never a substitute for — ASV.
